slides.title: The big idea
slides.html:
A deductive system is built in layers: undefined terms, then definitions, then postulates accepted without proof, then theorems proved from what came before.

Each theorem points back to its "parents," the facts its proof used. Euclid built his Elements this way around 300 BCE, starting from five postulates and a few common notions. If a theorem's proof uses only earlier results, the whole structure is as reliable as its starting postulates.
